title: The case for climate realism in an age of soaring energy demand
gist: Dieter Helm argues the energy-GDP 'decoupling' was an illusion created by offshoring heavy industry to coal-powered China, and that the Jevons paradox plus a new AI-driven energy-intensive industrial revolution point to roughly a doubling of energy demand by 2050. 'Climate realism' means accepting 2°C will be breached, prioritising adaptation, and recognising Europe's high-cost intermittent power is losing the new industries to the US and China.

insights.claim: The apparent decoupling of GDP growth from energy demand in Europe since the 1990s was largely a compositional shift: energy-intensive industries moved to China and Southeast Asia while global demand kept rising.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Treat European energy-intensity declines as carbon leakage, not structural efficiency; global fossil demand is the relevant metric.

insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Structural headwind for European energy-intensive manufacturers; policy backlash risk on renewables subsidies.

themes.theme: Jevons and the new energy-hungry economy

insights.claim: Energy efficiency acts like a fall in the price of energy, so it raises rather than lowers total energy demand (the Jevons paradox), which punctures demand-side decarbonisation narratives.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Do not model efficiency gains (including more efficient AI chips) as reducing aggregate power demand.
insights.quote: This is the Jevons paradox and it is rock solid.

insights.claim: Economies are undergoing a shift to new energy-intensive industries on a scale not seen since steel in the late 19th century, overwhelmingly requiring firm electricity.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Supports long-duration demand growth for firm generation: gas, nuclear, hydro, and grid infrastructure.
insights.locator: To this is added a further blow

insights.claim: AI industries need 'five nines' (99.999%) reliable power, which intermittent wind and solar cannot supply; electrification does not imply renewables since fossil fuels still provide about 85% of global energy.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Data-centre power will lean on dispatchable sources; favours gas turbines, nuclear, and firming assets over pure-play intermittent renewables.
insights.quote: intermittent generators like wind and solar do not meet the new AI industries’ demand for the five nines

insights.claim: Even if an AI bubble bursts under debt and valuation pressure, the technology will persist, just as electricity rollout survived the 1929 crash and social media survived the dot-com crash.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: A tech equity correction would be a temporary pause, not an end, for AI-linked power demand; long-dated energy infrastructure theses survive a crash.
insights.quote: The Great Crash in 1929 did not stop the electricity rollout, and the dot-com crash did not halt the coming of social media.

insights.claim: At 3% annual global growth, the world economy doubles by 2050, and 3% is below projected growth for China, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, much of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.

insights.claim: Even if the fossil-fuel share of global energy halved from 85%, a doubled world economy would keep absolute fossil fuel burn roughly flat.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Share-of-mix headlines mislead; absolute hydrocarbon volumes, which drive producer revenues, can hold up through 2050.

insights.claim: It is reasonable to assume the world will still burn at least 100 million barrels of oil a day in 2050, more gas than today, and still a lot of coal, helped by petrochemicals growth.
insights.speaker: Dieter Helm
insights.so_what: Contradicts peak-oil-demand-by-2030 narratives; supportive of long-cycle upstream oil and gas and LNG investment.
